body.p: This study presents a helpful approach for systematically assessing the effects of disease-relevant 5′- and 3′-UTR variants on translation using massively parallel polysome profiling. The evidence supporting the ability of this method to identify variants that alter polysome association is solid. The work provides a valuable resource and methodological framework for investigating noncoding variants and will be of interest to researchers studying translational regulation and variant function.

The authors describe a massively parallel reporter assays (MPRA) screen focused at identifying polymorphisms in 5' and 3' UTRs that affect translation efficiency and thus might have a functional impact on cells. The topic is of timely interest, and indeed, several related efforts have recently been published and preprinted (e.g., https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37516102/ and https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10635273/).
Comments on revisions:
The authors have now repeated the screen and collected new data that is high quality. From my perspective the manuscript has improved and I don't have any standing issues remaining.
The following is the authors’ response to the previous reviews.

disp-quote.p: The authors describe a massively parallel reporter assays (MPRA) screen focused at identifying polymorphisms in 5' and 3' UTRs that affect translation efficiency and thus might have a functional impact on cells. The topic is of timely interest, and indeed, several related efforts have recently been published and preprinted (e.g., https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37516102/ and https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10635273/). This study has several major issues with the results and their presentation.

The main issue remains that it appears that the screen has largely failed, and the reasons for that remain unclear, which make it difficult to interpret how useful is the resulting data. The authors mention batch effects as a potential contributor. The authors start with a library that includes ~6,000 variants, which makes it a medium-size MPRA. But then, only 483 pairs of WT/mutated UTRs yield high confidence information, which is already a small number for any downstream statistical analysis, particularly since most don't actually affect translation in the reporter screen setting (which is not unexpected). It is unclear why >90% of the library did not give high-confidence information. The profiles presented as base-case examples in Fig. 2B don't look very informative or convincing. All the subsequent analysis is done on a very small set of UTRs that have an effect, and it is unclear to this reviewer how these can yield statistically significant and/or biologically-relevant associations.

body.p: We recognize that RNA distribution within polysomes is inherently less stable than the associated protein components. This instability has been noted in previous studies, including those cited by the reviewer, which used RNA from bulk polysomes to infer the translatome without fractionation. Acknowledging this limitation, we purposely adopted a conservative strategy: (i) performing gross fractionation of polysomes, and (ii) collaborating with biostatisticians at the Institute of Statistical Science, Academia Sinica, to design a conservative yet optimized analysis pipeline that minimized batch effects.

To better illustrate the observed differences, we revised Fig. 2B to show the summarized proportions across fractions with error bars, allowing clearer visualization of the differences between genotypes.

From our high-confidence dataset, we applied a well-established statistical framework specifically designed to accommodate multiple influencing factors in relatively small datasets (Elements of Statistical Learning by Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman). We further conducted sensitivity analyses to select an optimal QC cutoff across a range of stringencies, ensuring maximal reliability of our results. We have therefore successfully shortlisted UTR variants which have strong effect on translation.

Building upon these conservative measures, we developed a predictive model for translation effects of UTR variants. Importantly, this model was validated not only with our internal test dataset but also with independent external datasets. In addition, the sequence features identified by the model were validated through reporter assays and in vivo CRISPR editing. These external and functional validations establish the generalizability and robustness of our approach.

disp-quote.p: From the variants that had an effect, the authors go on to carry out some protein-level validations, and see some changes, but it is not clear if those changes are in the same direction was observed in the screen. In their rebuttal the authors explain that they largely can not infer directionality of changes form the screen, which further limits its utility.

body.p: To determine the direction of polysome shifting, we repeated polysome profiling of the UTR libraries, separating transcripts into free RNA, 40S, and fractions containing 1–8 ribosomes (See Fig. 7A). Following established approaches, we used log2 [polysome (F2–F8)/ (free + 40S)] as an estimate of translational efficiency. This measure showed a strong correlation with translational efficiency determined by luciferase activity normalized to RNA expression (Spearman r = 0.744; See Fig. 7B). We then used this measure to assign the direction of polysome shifting (increased or decreased) to the significant variants (Supplemental Table S4).

Because the contribution of 5’ UTRs to translation was more evident than that of 3’ UTRs, we further used the estimated ribosome load of WT 5’ UTR sequences to construct a multivariable model explaining variation in 5’ UTR translational efficiency (Fig. 7C). The model significantly explained ribosome load in held-out data and was further supported by independent reporter transfections, in which model-derived values correlated with luciferase output (Spearman r = 0.762; Fig. 7D, E).
We have modified the main text to describe these measurements and modeling analyses (p. 23–24):
“Modeling the polysome occupancy of 5’ UTRs

Because 5’ UTRs contain multiple features, including RBP-binding motifs and RNA folding energy, that may jointly influence translation, we next asked whether these features could explain variation in polysome occupancy. We performed high-resolution polysome profiling of the UTR library, separating transcripts into free RNA (Free), 40S, monosome (1 ribosome), and polysome fractions containing 2-8 ribosomes (Fig. 7A). We evaluated several metrics of ribosome association and found that the polysome fraction normalized to the free and 40S fractions [Poly/ (Free + 40S)] showed the strongest agreement with the change in translational efficiency between WT and mutant pairs measured using luciferase reporters (Spearman r = 0.744) (Figs. 3 and 7B). We therefore used this index as a quantitative measure of polysome occupancy and assigned the direction of occupancy change (increased or decreased) for each polysome-shifting variant (Supplemental Table S4).

To identify 5’ UTR features associated with polysome occupancy, we first selected representative features from highly correlated feature groups (for example, CG dinucleotide frequency and overall GC content) and then applied standardized multivariable regression to estimate their relative effects, statistical significance, and confidence intervals (see Methods). Of the 2,850 WT 5’ UTRs in the library, 2,362 passed the read-depth and quality-control criteria and were included in the model. The resulting model revealed positive associations of GC-rich k-mers with polysome occupancy. GA-repeat motifs recognized by SRSF-family proteins were also positively associated with polysome occupancy (Fig. 7C), consistent with their enrichment among polysome-shifting UTR variants identified independently in our variant analysis (Figs. 4 and 5).

The multivariable model significantly explained variation in the observed polysome occupancy (Fig. 7D, Supplemental Table S4). Moreover, model derived polysome occupancy highly correlated with luciferase activity measured independently across eight WT 5’ UTRs (Spearman r = 0.762) (Fig. 7E), providing functional support for the relationships captured by the model. Together, these results identify sequence and regulatory features associated with 5’ UTR-dependent ribosome loading and provide a quantitative framework linking UTR composition and RBP-binding motifs to translational output.”
The corresponding experimental and modeling details have also been added to the Methods section (p. 7-8 and 14-16).

disp-quote.p: It is particularly puzzling how the authors can build a machine learning predictor with >3,000 features when the dataset they use for training the model has just a few dozens of translation-shifting variants.

body.p: Starting with variants that passed our stringent quality-control criteria, we applied a statistical framework suited for evaluating multiple features in relatively small datasets (Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning). We also systematically varied the QC threshold to assess the robustness of the results across different filtering stringencies. Importantly, the resulting findings were supported by independent reporter assays and further validated using an external dataset, demonstrating their reproducibility across experimental platforms and datasets.

disp-quote.p: It appears that the authors have extracted the information they could from the problematic dataset they obtained. Repeating the experiments in a cleaner setting, obtaining data for the >6000 UTRs they intended will allow the authors to achieve the goals they set out to achieve in establishing the screen.

body.p: We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comments. In response, we repeated polysome profiling of the UTR library. The repeated experiment not only reproduced the overall results of our initial screen but also provided additional information on the distribution of UTRs in the free RNA and 40S fractions. Using these data, we derived a polysome association index [Poly/ (Free + 40S)], which showed strong agreement with translational efficiency independently measured using individually transfected luciferase reporters. Together with the extensive additional analyses and revisions described above, these new data substantially strengthen the experimental foundation of our study and provide a more quantitative framework for interpreting the effects of UTR variants on translation.
We sincerely thank the reviewer for this constructive comment, which helped us improve the rigor and overall quality of the study.
